subtitle: A snapshot of which ARPANET hosts answered test connections between 28 February and 10 March 1972.

tldr.problem: People on the early Network needed to know which hosts were up and offering service, since many sites were unreliable or only intended for users.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested hosts daily from its Terminal IMP, recorded each result as a single letter such as O, D, H or T, and combined the results with each site's own status and predictions.
tldr.outcome: The report is a dated snapshot. The index lists it as obsoleting RFC 315 and as updated by RFC 326.

today: RFC 319 is a dated status report. The index lists it as obsoleting RFC 315 and as updated by RFC 326, and its status is recorded as unknown.

sections.title: What the Report Covers
sections.content:
Ellen Westheimer of BBN reports on the status of most Network Hosts from February 28 to March 10, 1972. During this period the ETAC Terminal IMP (Network address 148) was installed.

Several hosts are left out of the daily testing. One group is not expected to work as servers on a regular basis for at least two weeks, namely MIT-AI (134), Case (13) and Ames/(Paoli) (15). The other group is intended for users only, including the Terminal IMPs, the Network Control Center computer (address 5) used solely for gathering statistics, and Rand (7), Harvard (73), Illinois (12) and NBS (19).
sections.eli5: The note says which computers were checked every day and which were left off the list because they were not meant to be visited.

sections.title: Site Status and Predictions
sections.content:
The first table lists each host by Network address, site and computer, with a status or prediction and the person it was obtained from. Entries include Server, Server (Exper.), User Only, Never, a month such as June or September, and the quoted word "Soon". A footnote says the UCLA NMC is a research site that would like prior arrangement with each user.

The UCLA IBM-360/91 offered only a Network Job Service (NETRJS) at the time, with Telnet expected in April. The BBN test setup could not test NETRJS, so a connection to the NETRJS logger was taken to mean it was working.
sections.eli5: This is the big list of who is who: which computers are helpers, which are only for visitors, and which say they will be ready soon.

sections.title: The Daily Test Codes
sections.content:
The second table shows test results by site on dates from 2/28 to 3/10, each tested from the BBN Terminal IMP at a recorded Eastern time. The letters mean the following. Sites flagged with a hash sign advertise they may not have their system available at that time.

  • D Dead: the host was dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP.
  • H Half open: the host opened a connection but then closed it or went silent.
  • O Open: the host opened a connection and was accessible to users.
  • R Refused: the host returned a CLS to the initial RFC.
  • T Timed out: the host did not complete the ICP and open a connection within 60 seconds.
sections.eli5: Each computer got a one-letter grade, like open, closed, asleep or too slow to answer.

items.label: Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection and was accessible to users.

items.label: 1/2 Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection, then closed it or did not respond.

items.label: Timed out
items.desc: No ICP completed and no connection opened within 60 seconds.

items.label: Refused
items.desc: Host returned a CLS to the initial RFC.

items.label: Dead
items.desc: Host dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP.
